content: Microcytic anemia is a condition in which red blood cells are smaller than normal. In microcytic anemia, the MCV is less than 76 fl. Conversely, when the MCV is greater than 100 fl, the condition is referred to as macrocytic anemia. In addition to being smaller in size, the red blood cells in microcytic anemia are often hypochromic, meaning they appear paler than normal. This paleness is due to a reduced amount of hemoglobin within the cells. The normal range for MCH is 27-32 picograms (pg). The normal range for MCHC is approximately 320-360 grams per liter (g/L) or 32-36 grams per deciliter (g/dL). As a result, microcytic anemia is typically described as microcytic, hypochromic anemia. The most common cause of this condition is iron deficiency anemia, which is the leading cause of anemia overall and the most frequent cause of microcytic anemia specifically. Other causes include thalassemia, a group of inherited blood disorders; sideroblastic anemia, which can be either congenital or acquired; and, less commonly, anemia of chronic disease, although this more often results in normochromic, normocytic anemia. Rarely, lead poisoning can also lead to microcytic anemia. It is important to note that other conditions typically associated with normocytic or macrocytic anemia may also need to be considered, as the presence of multiple causes of anemia can alter the expected clinical presentation.
